New `sendSubagentChunkWs` wrapper in `client-wrapper.ts` standardizes WebSocket action dispatching. Updated `evals/scaffolding.ts` to provide the new dependency, ensuring test parity with production runtime.

eli5.text: When the assistant is working with a helper agent and sends you little updates in chunks, that sending step is now set up the same way during automated tests as it works during your real session, so the test environment matches how your actual assistant behaves. The underlying behavior for you has not changed yet; this is housekeeping that keeps the testing setup consistent with the production runtime.

ai.title: Fix typechecker in test and evals agent runtime

eli5.text: The internal testing tools that let the system run practice runs of the assistant now load up correctly, so developers no longer hit a type-checking error when building or running those practice scenarios. The team also added a placeholder for streaming assistant responses in those same testing tools, which means the test environment is now structurally ready to mimic a feature the live system already supports, even though that placeholder simply raises an error if called today. If you looked at the testing setup, you'd see the definitions are written in a way that matches the real system's expectations, and there's a new stub entry listed alongside the other response-related pieces.

ai.title: Add BuffBench nightly evals
ai.summary: Nightly CI runs `run-buffbench-nightly` instead of `run-eval-set`. New `evals/buffbench/main-nightly.ts` executes `runBuffBench` on `base` and `base2` agents, then emails formatted scores. Scope: `.github/workflows/nightly-evals.yml`, `evals/package.json`, new nightly script. Email content includes average score, cost, duration, and valid run count per agent.

eli5.text: Each night, the system now runs a specialized evaluation routine that tests how two specific versions of the assistant (called "base" and "base2") perform on a set of benchmark tasks, then automatically emails a summary of the results to the team. Previously, the nightly automation ran a more general evaluation tool. This new process specifically executes performance and cost measurements for those two assistant versions and sends the formatted scores via email, so the team gets a direct comparison of their nightly performance without needing to dig into logs.

ai.title: Inject handleStepsLogChunk into AgentRuntimeScopedDeps
ai.summary: Added `handleStepsLogChunk` to `AgentRuntimeScopedDeps` and `client.ts` contracts, replacing direct `sendAction` calls in `run-programmatic-step.ts`. This decouples step logging from WebSocket transport by injecting a scoped handler via `WebSocketMiddleware`. Updates include new `handleStepsLogChunkWs` in `client-wrapper.ts` and test stubs in `agent-runtime.ts`.

eli5.text: If you watched an assistant work on a coding task, its behind-the-scenes log lines used to go out over the live connection as they happened. Now that log streaming is handed off to a reusable plug-in module instead of being hardwired to the connection, so the same logging logic can be swapped for other transports or tests later. Right now, what you see is the same: the logs still arrive live. The difference is only visible in the code that wires the pieces together.

eli5.text: The way the assistant replaces text in files was quietly rewritten so it fits the rest of the codebase better, with no change to how it actually works. If you swap text in a file today, it still behaves exactly as before; you just won't notice anything different. This was behind-the-scenes housekeeping to keep things consistent for the engineering team.

ai.summary: evals/scaffolding.ts now imports handleStepsLogChunkWs and wires it into AgentRuntimeScopedDeps. Fixes typecheck errors from missing handler. Internal evals surface only.

eli5.text: The internal testing tools for the assistant's automated checks now properly handle a specific kind of log it produces when working through multi-step problems. Previously, a piece of the evals setup was missing this handler, which caused the test-time type-checker to fail; wiring it into the runtime dependencies for evals restores correct type-checking during those internal evaluations. If you look at the evals scaffolding, you'd see this handler now passed in alongside the other mocked workspace operations. This affects only internal automated evaluations and is already in place today, doing nothing for end users.

Engineers rewrote how one helper function is defined, switching it from a compact inline form to a standard named function, then applied the same compatibility check in a separate statement instead of attaching it directly. This is internal housekeeping only, so you won't see any change in how saving files works today or in the future; it just keeps things organized for the team maintaining the code.

If you watched the assistant work behind the scenes, you would see it no longer switches between two different search tools depending on the task, it just uses the regular one every time. This affects only the internal setup that controls which helpers the assistant is allowed to use, and it is live today.

The change quietly added a flag so handlesteps skip the usual tool-allowlist check, letting them execute any available tool instead of being limited to the ones pre-approved in the configuration. You wouldn't see anything different unless you were running handlesteps, in that case, tools that were previously blocked will now work. Whoever has access to handlesteps today now effectively gains broader tool access; that access changed as of this update.

Instead of being reminded to summarize what it did, it now focuses only on getting the job done and checking off the remaining steps. The main control assistant now explicitly delegates to the new editing and review assistants during normal operation. If you looked, you'd see fresh definitions for planning, editing, and reviewing roles that all point to the same newer model instead of the previous default.

eli5.text: The behind-the-scenes communication between different parts of the system has been reorganized so that shared tools like logging and sending responses are passed around more consistently. This touch-up spans several core backend areas and cleans up duplicated wiring, but you wouldn't see any change in how the product behaves today; it is purely internal housekeeping to make future updates easier and less error-prone for the team building the system.

eli5.text: You can now ask the codebase assistant to find files for you using a lighter, faster model, and it will locate the most relevant files without doing text searches. The system now routes file-discovery tasks to this new setup, so results should focus on file locations and brief relevance notes rather than deep code analysis. This caused a small mismatch where the system couldn't quite place which specific file-fetching helper was being asked for. Now it correctly introduces itself as "file-picker-max," so the system can tell it apart from any simpler file-picking helpers. If you looked at the settings behind the scenes, you'd see the name tag on this particular helper now matches what it's actually supposed to do.

Covers backend LLM APIs. `saveMessage` now receives `cacheReadInputTokens`, `cacheCreationInputTokens`, and `costOverrideDollars` from OpenRouter metadata.

eli5.text: Relace apply, the internal tool that handles code edits, has switched to using a new model provider called OpenRouter instead of hitting Relace's own endpoint directly. If you're an internal user or developer relying on Relace apply's backend behavior, the assistant now routes requests through OpenRouter using a model named relace/relace-apply-3. Behind the scenes, the system now tracks extra details like cached input tokens and cost overrides pulled from OpenRouter's response metadata, which affects how message costs are recorded. The switch is live today in the backend, and users of the apply feature themselves should notice no visible difference.

ai.summary: Removed messageId from fastRewrite params and promptRelaceAI call. Updated ParamsExcluding type to exclude only initialCode. Fixes process-file-block.test.ts.

ai.title: Initial CLI app with proper TUI
ai.summary: New `cli` package introduces a terminal UI with chat components, multiline input, and branch items. Backend updates propagate `parentAgentId` and `forwardToPrompt` flags through subagent streaming and spawn handlers to support nested agent contexts in the new interface. Files include `cli/src/chat.tsx`, `backend/src/run-programmatic-step.ts`, and `backend/src/tools/handlers/tool/spawn-agents.ts`.

eli5.text: You can now launch a new terminal-based chat interface for the assistant that renders rich formatting and supports multi-line input and nested sub-agents. Behind the scenes, the streaming pipeline now tags every response chunk with which agent produced it (via parentAgentId and forwardToPrompt flags) so that conversations involving several layers of helper-agents display correctly in the new terminal UI. Live today as an initial release: open the terminal, start the new interface, and you'll see styled markdown messages and branched agent conversations instead of plain text. The developers warn that the terminal UI is strict about how spaces and text elements are written, so misusing them can blank the whole screen.
